title: Penalty Is Better Than Punishment
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece draws a precise distinction between penalties (losing something you already have) and punishments (being made to do something distasteful), arguing that leaders conflate the two despite their different communicative effects. Penalties, the author argues, are more effective because they're typically pre-established and known in advance, so they reinforce standards proactively rather than punishing after the fact. The piece recommends that leaders pre-set clear penalties for known rule violations so they can spend their energy reinforcing good behavior instead of inventing consequences reactively.
points: A penalty takes something away (compensation, access, status); a punishment requires doing something undesired — and the two send different signals.
Pre-established, known penalties communicate standards proactively, so people focus on upholding rules rather than avoiding getting caught.
Punishments, by contrast, only signal what not to do case-by-case, which is why they often produce evasion rather than genuine behavior change.
Leaders who set clear penalties in advance can spend their time reinforcing desired behavior instead of continually inventing new deterrents.
quotes: A penalty requires you to lose something you already have, whereas a punishment makes you engage in something you don’t want to.
But penalties send a better message than do punishments. When others receive penalties, they show the team what standards, rules, or values cannot be violated.
When everyone knows and understands the penalties for serious infractions, they generally accept them and focus on upholding the rules rather than avoiding the missteps.
This is why people often devise creative ways of not being caught rather than changing their behavior.
Once set, it is the team and not the leader who imposes them.
